US commercial insurance claims, 2013–2015 (796,330 people aged 16–64): sustained gabapentin overuse without opioid overuse, against gabapentin without overuse, all-cause hospital admission OR 1.366 (95% CI 1.055–1.769) and drug-related admission 1.440 (1.010–2.053); sustained gabapentin overuse with sustained opioid overuse (comparison group not stated in the review), all-cause admission 4.083 (2.582–6.457) and emergency or inpatient care for respiratory depression 4.106 (1.753–9.619). Listed limitations include possible residual confounding and claims that may not reflect consumption; adjustment is not described.

The abstract concludes that evidence suggests gabapentinoid misuse is a growing trend causing significant patient harm (the Discussion, 4.6, states this without the hedge), and the Conclusion, also prefaced by 'evidence suggests', calls the trend alarming; the Discussion says the harm seen with gabapentinoids taken with opioids was not limited to people with substance use disorders or to misuse. Limitations: highly heterogeneous studies, hence a qualitative synthesis only; limited generalisability (small samples, single sites, a focus on substance use disorder or overdose cohorts rather than the general population); retrospective designs; reliance on surrogate markers of misuse and harm; and the assumption of a class effect, that findings for one gabapentinoid apply to the other.

In its paragraph on gabapentinoid misuse, the introduction gives a lifetime prevalence in the general population of 2.5%, based on a 2013 UK study; its reference 5 is Kapil et al. (2014), Br J Clin Pharmacol 78(1):190–1, on misuse of the GABA analogues baclofen, gabapentin and pregabalin in the UK. The review gives no per-drug figures for that survey (editors' reading: since the cited source also covers baclofen, the 2.5% may not be for gabapentinoids alone).

evidence_set: The probabilities within the first year, the first decade and over a lifetime are 'estimated projections' by the standard actuarial method and are printed without intervals; the Methods mention 95% intervals for the weighted frequencies describing the sample (Tables 1 and 2 print none), and the hazard ratios in Tables 3 and 4 carry 95% intervals. Limits the authors state: substance use and disorders self-reported, not confirmed by objective methods; recall bias, greater the longer ago the event, and cognitive impairment from drug use; intermittent use making the time from first use to dependence inexact; institutionalized people, who have an increased probability of a dependence diagnosis, excluded; income not available as a covariate that changes over time.

evidence_set: Death, and among rats that died the time from the start of the injection to death, were the only outcomes: no breathing, blood level or other measure of tolerance was taken at any point. The authors propose a model of overdose deaths in which tolerance fails where the drug is given in an environment not previously associated with it, describe the design as a methodologically rigorous demonstration of the contribution of contextual stimuli to tolerance, read the DT-ST difference as showing that identical drug histories need not produce equal tolerance to heroin's lethal effect, and conclude that rats given the high dose among cues previously associated with lower doses were more likely to survive than rats given it among cues not associated with the drug. The abstract says the results suggest that conditioned drug-anticipatory responses, besides pharmacological factors, affect heroin-induced mortality. No human data are reported.
